draft.title: The Atlantic slave trade and abolition
card: From the 1500s to the 1800s, European traders shipped millions of Africans across the Atlantic Ocean. They were sold as slaves to work on plantations and in mines in the Americas.
Enslaved people resisted in many ways, from working slowly and escaping to open revolt. A revolt in Haiti in the 1790s ended slavery there and led to its independence.
Reformers, many of them former slaves, also campaigned in Britain. They wrote books, spoke at meetings and organised petitions and boycotts of slave-grown goods.
Abolition means ending something by law. Britain made the slave trade illegal in 1807. It then ended slavery in most of its colonies in 1833.
draft.remember: Abolition came from resistance by enslaved people and from reform campaigns. Britain banned the trade first, then slavery.

a.q: What did Britain's law of 1807 do?
opts: Made the slave trade illegal
Freed all slaves in British colonies
Ended slavery across the whole world
Made the slave trade legal only on ships
a.why: The 1807 law banned the trade, which meant shipping people as slaves. It did not free those already enslaved. That came in 1833, and only in most British colonies.
a.clue: Think about trade first, and slavery later.

b.q: Which statement best explains why Britain ended slavery in its colonies?
opts: Resistance and reform campaigns built pressure for change
Enslaved people had already won freedom in every colony
Plantation owners asked Parliament to end slavery
Other countries forced Britain to pass the law
b.why: Revolts and escapes by enslaved people, together with reformers' petitions and boycotts, pushed Britain to act. Slavery was not already over in 1833, and the card gives no sign that plantation owners or other countries drove the law.
b.clue: Look at what enslaved people and reformers did.

b.best: Resistance and reform campaigns built pressure for change

problems.detail: 'Reformers, many of them former slaves' overstates it. Some formerly enslaved people, such as Olaudah Equiano, Ottobah Cugoano and Mary Prince, campaigned in Britain, but most British reformers were not former slaves (for example Quakers, Clarkson and Wilberforce). Use 'some of them former slaves'.

check.summary: The card says 'many' British reformers were former slaves, which overstates it; 'some' is accurate. Both questions and the explanations are otherwise sound.
